Four bills promulgated by the California legislature are highlighted in Table A1: Senate Bill (SB) 100 (SB100, De León, Chapter 312, Statutes of 2018); SB49 (Skinner, Chapter 697, Statutes of 2019); Assembly Bill (AB) 205 (AB205, Chapter 61, Statutes of 2022), and SB 846 (Dodd, Chapter 239, Statutes of 2022). Here we provide brief overviews of the main provisions of these bills of relevance to load flexibility. SB100 establishes the context in which load flexibility is an important aspect of grid reliability. SB100 accelerated the existing Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS) obligations for “retail sellers” in California, defined as IOUs, publicly owned utilities (POUs), energy service providers (ESPs),23 and CCAs. It adjusted the RPS obligations as follows: (a) from 40% to 44% by 2024; (b) from 45% to 52% by 2027; and (c) from 50% to 60% by 2030. SB100 also established that 100% of all retail sales of electricity to California end-use customers be supplied by RPS-eligible and zero-carbon resources by December 31, 2045. SB49 (Skinner, Chapter 697, Statutes of 2019) is much more directly focused on load flexibility. It modifies the CEC’s regulatory authority to allow the agency to establish and periodically update appliance energy efficiency standards which promote the diffusion and use of flexible demand technologies which help to maintain electrical grid reliability. SB49 required that the called-for “flexible demand appliance standards” (FDAS) be based on “feasible and attainable efficiencies or feasible improvements enabling appliance operations to be scheduled, shifted, or curtailed” to reduce the GHGs associated with electricity generation. AB205 (Chapter 61, Statutes of 2022) included several statutory changes considered necessary to implement the energy related items of the 2022 Budget Act, three of which were particularly noteworthy for dynamic prices and load flexibility.
